content: Buffered Penicillin G Potassium for Injection, USP, can be administered either intravenously or intramuscularly. The specific dosage and administration guidelines are as follows: 1. Pediatric Patients: This medication should not be administered to pediatric patients requiring less than one million units per dose. Refer to the Precautions – Pediatric Use section for further details. 2. Renal Impairment: Penicillin G is generally non-toxic, and dosage adjustments are typically necessary only in cases of severe renal impairment. For patients with a creatinine clearance of less than 10 mL/min, administer a full loading dose (as per the recommended dosages) followed by half the loading dose every 8 to 10 hours. For patients with a creatinine clearance of 10 to 50 mL/min, administer a full loading dose followed by half the loading dose every 4 to 5 hours. Additional dosage modifications may be required for patients with both hepatic disease and renal impairment. 3. Duration of Therapy: For most acute infections, treatment should continue for at least 48 to 72 hours after the patient becomes asymptomatic. In cases of Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infections, antibiotic therapy should be maintained for at least 10 days to reduce the risk of rheumatic fever. 4. Inspection of Parenteral Products: Prior to administration, parenteral drug products should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration whenever the solution and container allow. Preparation of Solution: To prepare the solution, loosen the powder in the vial. Hold the vial horizontally and rotate it while slowly directing the stream of diluent against the vial wall. After adding all the diluent, shake the vial vigorously. Depending on the route of administration, use Sterile Water for Injection, USP, or Sterile Isotonic Sodium Chloride Solution for Parenteral use. Note: Penicillins are rapidly inactivated in the presence of carbohydrate solutions at an alkaline pH. Reconstitution: The amount of solvent required for reconstitution depends on the desired concentration. If the required volume of solvent exceeds the vial's capacity, dissolve the penicillin by injecting only a portion of the solvent into the vial, then withdraw the resultant solution and combine it with the remaining solvent in a larger sterile container. Penicillin G Potassium for Injection, USP, is highly water-soluble and can be dissolved in small amounts of Water for Injection or Sterile Isotonic Sodium Chloride Solution for Parenteral Use. All solutions should be stored in a refrigerator. When refrigerated, penicillin solutions can be stored for up to seven days without significant loss of potency. Administration Routes: 1. Intramuscular Injection: Keep the total injection volume small. The intramuscular route is the preferred method of administration. Solutions containing up to 100,000 units of penicillin per mL of diluent may be used with minimal discomfort. Higher concentrations are physically possible and may be employed when therapy demands. For large doses, it may be advisable to administer aqueous solutions of penicillin via continuous intravenous drip. 2. Continuous Intravenous Drip: Determine the volume of fluid and the rate of administration required by the patient over a 24-hour period, as per standard fluid therapy practices. Add the appropriate daily dosage of penicillin to this fluid. For example, if an adult patient requires 2 liters of fluid in 24 hours and a daily dosage of 10 million units of penicillin, add 5 million units to 1 liter and adjust the flow rate so that the liter is infused over 12 hours. 3. Intrapleural or Other Local Infusion: If fluid is aspirated, administer the infusion in a volume equal to 1/4 or 1/2 the amount of fluid aspirated. Otherwise, prepare the solution as for an intramuscular injection. 4. Intrathecal Use: The intrathecal use of penicillin in meningitis must be highly individualized. This route should only be employed with full consideration of the potential irritating effects of penicillin. The preferred route of therapy in bacterial meningitis is intravenous administration, supplemented by intramuscular injection. Dosage for High-Unit Administration: Buffered Penicillin G Potassium for Injection can be administered intramuscularly or by continuous intravenous drip for dosages of 500,000, 1,000,000, or 5,000,000 units. It is also suitable for intrapleural, intraarticular, and other local installations. The 20,000,000-unit (20 million unit) dosage may only be administered via intravenous infusion.
